 Dropping your captain, the man that has held the team together for most of the past five years, is a bold move from a man whose job is on the line. It was very much a make-or-break decision from Michael Carrick to leave out Bruno Fernandes against Bournemouth. It did not work, and Carrick knew the consequences if it failed and will probably pay the price for it, but he should not be alone.
 Carrick said the decision to drop Fernandes was purely based on football reasons but criticising his manager after the desperate defeat to Como cannot have helped. Clearly Carrick disagreed with his captain’s comments on the lack of pressing in the Champions League fixture. It was somewhat telling that Lisandro Martínez kept his place despite pointing out the director of football, Jason Wilcox, was a hindrance to the club the previous week.
 Fernandes has been a long way from his best this season, with three goals and one assist in the Premier League, all in one game against Ipswich . It would have been justifiable to give someone else an opportunity in the No 10 role, especially when the squad contains far too many of those. But then, no one at United is in form, so keeping an angry Fernandes in position may have made more sense. United have won almost half the Premier League fixtures Fernandes has started since he joined in 2020, and less than a third when he is absent.
 Fernandes gamble leaves Carrick to carry the can for United’s institutional failures | Will Unwin Read more Share 16m ago 14.25 EDT Sunderland stay bottom of the Premier League table, but it would be foolish to read too much into a game that was played in vile conditions. Both sides tried their best and had periods of dominance. Leeds almost nicked it at the end when Sean Longstaff’s shot was blocked on the line. But they had to settle for a point, which makes it five draws from eight games this season. They remain extremely tough to beat.

 And the winner is… the wind.

 Ampadu’s deep cross is driven back into the middle by Okafor. Longstaff, the former Newcastle man, hits a low shot from six yards that is somehow blocked in the six-yard box, I think by O’Nien. The keeper Roefs was completely out of the game.

 Share 23m ago 14.18 EDT 90 min Longstaff curls a low shot from 22 yards that is pushed round the post by the sprawling Roefs. That’s a good save at full stretch because it was a precise effort from Longstaff.

 Update: he’s fine.

 Share 36m ago 14.05 EDT 76 min Now Leeds are having a spell of pressure. Roefs spills Tanaka’s shot on the turn and dives at the feet of Calvert-Lewin, who goes flying. O’Nien was lunging towards the ball as well. No penalty, and no intervention from VAR. I’d like to see that again as I think Calvert-Lewin got the first touch; whether he was fouled is another matter.

 Share 46m ago 13.55 EDT 67 min Bogle is booked for a clumsy high challenge on Reinildo. The home fans wanted more but it won’t be upgraded by VAR.

 Share 53m ago 13.47 EDT 60 min Rigg, found by Xhaka, slithers into the area from the right and has a left-foot shot blocked. Leeds break and Bogle’s shot is also blocked.

 Brian Brobbey may also have a problem – his movement looks a bit laboured.

 When football’s dignitaries assemble on Monday at the London Palladium for the Ballon d’Or ceremony it will be a far cry from the first awards 70 years ago. That was held in the slightly less glamorous surroundings of Blackpool town hall, where Stanley Matthews was presented with the prize by Gabriel Hanot, the visionary editor of L’Équipe who came up with the idea of crowning the world’s best player every year.
 A specially commissioned china plate was also handed over by the town’s mayor before the 41-year-old Matthews, who was famously teetotal, gave a short speech. “He might have had a double carrot juice that day,” says his son, Stanley Matthews Jr, who will attend this year’s awards with his sister, Jean, and her two daughters. “There was no ceremony. ‘Here’s your Ballon d’Or, well done’, sort of thing. But obviously it’s grown over the years, and now it’s a huge event. We’re very excited.”
 The switch of venue to England from its usual home in Paris is a mark of respect to the man who became the first active player to receive a knighthood in 1965, a few months before retiring at the age of 50. It also provides an opportunity to recall an astonishing career that began with his local side Stoke in 1932 and made the “Wizard of Dribble” the most famous player on the planet.
 Ballon d’Or ceremony returns to England in nod to ‘revolutionary’ Stanley Matthews Read more Share Updated at  13.26 EDT 1h ago 13.20 EDT “Most teams have one player whose absence makes them worse,” writes Kári Tulinius. “Usually it’s because, like with Enciso at Ipswich, it’s their best player. Without Brobbey, Sunderland are much diminished, but he’s not obviously in a different class. However, with his diligent harrying and intelligent movement, he creates space for his teammates. Even in a poor game he’s a joy to watch.”
 His hold-up play reminds me of Mark Hughes at Manchester United. You could throw any old filth at him and he would somehow control it, fight off four defenders and play the right pass.
 Share Updated at  13.26 EDT 1h ago 13.18 EDT Half time: Sunderland 0-0 Leeds
 That was hard work for the fans, never mind the players. A gale-force wind made it tricky to put more than a few passes together. The closest we came to a goal was when Brian Brobbey forced a short backpass and was denied by James Trafford.
